questions.prompt: How does the email confirmation token compare with the password reset token?
options: It is a 6-digit code the user types in, unlike the reset token
It is stored in `AspNetUserTokens`, unlike the reset token
It never expires, unlike the reset token
It is the same mechanism, with a different internal purpose string
questions.explanation: Email confirmation has the identical shape: a `SecurityStamp`-based token, URL-encoded into a link, with a frontend page in between. Only the purpose string differs (`"EmailConfirmation"` instead of `"ResetPassword"`).

source.section: Email confirmation — yes, same pattern as password reset

questions.prompt: How does the OTP pattern differ from the email confirmation link?
options: `GenerateTwoFactorTokenAsync` with `TokenOptions.DefaultEmailProvider` produces a short numeric code the user types in, so there is no link or URL encoding
OTP tokens are long encrypted blobs that must be URL-encoded twice
OTP codes are stored in plain text in the `AspNetUsers` table
OTP skips Identity's token machinery entirely and uses `Random`
questions.explanation: The OTP is sent as plain text and verified with `VerifyTwoFactorTokenAsync`. It still uses Identity's token machinery, but the email provider produces a short code rather than an encrypted blob.

source.section: OTP — completely different pattern, no link involved

questions.prompt: You set `Configure<DataProtectionTokenProviderOptions>(o => o.TokenLifespan = TimeSpan.FromHours(2))`. What is the effect?
options: Only password reset tokens last 2 hours
Only email confirmation tokens last 2 hours
Password reset and email confirmation tokens both last 2 hours
All tokens, including OTP codes and refresh tokens, last 2 hours
questions.explanation: Both token types come from `DataProtectorTokenProvider` and share its single options class, so one `TokenLifespan` applies to both. Independent lifespans need separate named providers.

questions.prompt: After registering a custom `"PasswordReset"` provider and generating tokens with `GenerateUserTokenAsync(user, "PasswordReset", "ResetPassword")`, why can't you just call `ResetPasswordAsync`?
options: `ResetPasswordAsync` only accepts tokens shorter than 6 characters
The built-in method is hardcoded to the default provider, so you verify with `VerifyUserTokenAsync` and reset the password manually
Custom providers can't be used for passwords at all
`ResetPasswordAsync` requires the old password as well
questions.explanation: `ResetPasswordAsync` and `ConfirmEmailAsync` look for tokens from the default provider under specific internal purpose strings, so tokens from custom-named providers aren't recognised.

source.section: Solution: register custom named providers, each with its own lifespan

questions.prompt: A system account has `LockoutEnabled = false`, and a script fails its password 10 times. What happens?
options: The account is locked for `DefaultLockoutTimeSpan` after the 5th failure
The account is locked permanently
`AccessFailedCount` stays at 0 because failures aren't counted
The failures are still counted, but `IsLockedOutAsync` stays false
questions.explanation: `LockoutEnabled` is a per-user switch. With it off, `AccessFailedAsync` still increments the counter, but no lockout is enforced.

questions.prompt: With `MaxFailedAccessAttempts = 5` and `LockoutEnabled = true`, what does `AccessFailedAsync` do on the 5th bad attempt?
options: Deletes the user's password so they must reset it
Increments the count and sets `LockoutEnd` to now plus `DefaultLockoutTimeSpan`
Resets `AccessFailedCount` to 0 without locking
Sets `LockoutEnabled` to false
questions.explanation: Once the count reaches the threshold, `AccessFailedAsync` calls `SetLockoutEndDateAsync(user, UtcNow.Add(DefaultLockoutTimeSpan))` for you. A user is locked out while `LockoutEnd` is in the future.
